This is an alternative to the view19,21 that membrane-bound cytochrome $\pmb { c }$ is lipid-linked and capable of rotating its ""active face" to different neighbouring reaction sites without forming long lived complexes with essentially "locked" configurations. Recent studies demonstrate the formation of other cytochrome c complexes, both with non-enzymatic proteins such as phosvitin22 and with active systems such as the photoreactive centre of Rhodopseudomonas spheroides23. The complex between cytochrome c and yeast peroxidase, if it is a catalytically active intermediate, is, however, the first functional complex to be defined in true solution. Other complexes with cytochrome c involve membrane fragments or detergent-solubilized enzymes. How does electron transfer occur within these complexes ? The ease with which both cytochrome $\pmb { c } ^ { 1 }$ and yeast peroxidase24 crystallize suggests that it may be possible to crystallize the two proteins together. X-ray analysis of such a crystal would give clues to the mode of electron transfer that cannot yet be obtained for the corresponding membranebound systems.

Target Size of DNA in Ultraviolet Irradiation

I reporT here a simple experimental observation which suggests that the rate of inactivation of bacteriophage by ultraviolet irradiation is proportional to the quantity of DNA, and that the cause of inactivation is, for the most part, interference with DNA replication.

A mutant of phage $\lambda ,$ , λb2, carries a large deletion in the central region of the chromosome. This region, which is not required for vegetative growth, comprises about $1 5 \%$ of the λ DNAi-3. If ultraviolet irradiation principally or only damages DNA, if ultraviolet-induced lesions in the b2 region are repaired with the same efficiency as lesions elsewhere, and if lesions in the b2 region are functionally the same as those elsewhere, then the ultraviolet sensitivities of $\lambda ^ { + }$ and λb2 should be proportional to the amount of DNA they contain. Photoreactivation and excision repair, both of which eliminate pyrimidine dimers from ultraviolet-irradiated DNA in vivo4,s, also greatly increase survival, which justifies the assumption that DNA is indeed the principal ultraviolet target. Pyrimidine dimers are the most important type of lethal lesion in ultraviolet irradiated $\lambda ^ { 6 }$ .

text: Fig. 1 shows inactivation curves of extracellularly ultraviolet irradiated $\lambda ^ { + }$ (closed symbols) and $\lambda b 2$ (open symbols), assayed on wild type $\scriptstyle { E . }$ coli AB1157 (circles), its excision repair deficient derivative AB1886 uvrA6 $( \nabla , \ \pmb { \eta } )$ , and the double excision and recombination deficient mutant AB2480 uvr A6 recA13 $( \triangle , \blacktriangle )$ .

All three bacterial assays show increased resistance to ultraviolet irradiation of λb2 as compared with $\lambda ^ { + }$ The dose increase, measured on the exponential part of the survival curves (as indicated in the figure), is about $1 7 \%$ when irradiated phage are assayed on either AB1157 or on AB1886 uvrA6, and $1 4 \%$ when assayed on AB2480 uvr A6 recA13. This is in good agreement with the results of physical measurements of $\lambda ^ { + }$ and λb2 DNA, which indicate that the b2 region comprises $1 8 \% ^ { 2 }$ and $1 3 \% ^ { 3 }$ of the $\lambda ^ { + }$ chromosome. X-ray irradiation gives results similar to those presented here (Arber and
Hradecna, cited in ref. 2, and personal communication from Arber).

It is not possible to exclude a priori the remote possibility that $\lambda ^ { + }$ is more sensitive to irradiation than λb2 because of some function of the b2 region. This region might, for example, code for an enzyme which inactivates irradiated XDNA. The improbability of such an explanation is enhanced by the exact correspondence between DNA content and ultraviolet sensitivity, which would then be a coincidence.

The correspondence between the DNA content and ultraviolet sensitivity of $\lambda ^ { + }$ and $\lambda b 2$ suggests that DNA is the principal or sole ultraviolet target, and that damage to the b2 region is both physically and functionally the same as damage elsewhere. This means that damage in the b2 region is repaired with the same efficiency as elsewhere; that the same fraction of lesions is irreparable in the b2 region as elsewhere (which further indicates that irreparable lesions are also DNA lesions); and that so far as ultraviolet inactivation is concerned, the entire chromosome, including the b2 region, has a similar indispensable function which is proportional to DNA content. It therefore seems that ultraviolet target size is directly proportional to the quantity of DNA irradiated, the function of the area being irrelevant.

Because the b2 region is not required for vegetative phage growth, it would be reasonable if this region were more or less immune to radiation damage. If this were true, $\lambda ^ { + }$ and λb2 would have very similar or identical sensitivities to ultraviolet irradiation. It could be that, as regards function, the b2 region is in fact relatively insensitive but that, fortuitously, it is physically more readily damaged or less readily repaired; and that these factors exactly compensate each other.

Otherwise, the similarity in functional sensitivity of the b2 region and the remainder of $\gimel$ chromosome must be related to the mechanism by which ultraviolet lesions inactivate the phage. Inactivation is presumably due to an effect on either DNA transcription or replication. Transcription of some early genes is required for the replication of infecting λDNA and for subsequent phage development7. The b2 region is transcribed7, but is not required for vegetative growth. With regard to transcription, therefore, ultraviolet lesions in this region can only affect viability if they prevent the transcription of other regions. This could result if transcription must toke place sequentially along the genome or parts of it, including the $^ { b 2 }$ region. But because the leftward and rightward transcriptions converge and terminate in the b2 region and because only a part of the genome is transcribed before DNA replication takes place7,8, it is unlikely that an effect on transcription would be proportional to the amount of DNA. It seems probable, therefore, that most inactivating ultraviolet lesions block not DNA transcription but DNA replication and that the primary inactivation event occurs on the level of DNA replication.

Coordination of Sex Pili with their Specifying R Factors

A sINGLE bacterial cell can simultaneously carry both F-like $( \hbar ^ { + } )$ and I-like (fi-) R factors and, when the R factors are de-repressed, most cells produce both F-like and I-like sex pili. These pili can be distinguished immunologically and by their capacity to adsorb different phages1. The $\mathbf { F }$ pilus is the receptor for RNA phages such as MS2 and filamentous DNA phages such as M13. The I pilus is the receptor for other filamentous DNA phages such as If1 and If2. Electron microscopy suggests that these filamentous DNA phages, both F-specific and I-specific, adsorb to the tip of the pilus2,3.

These experiments were designed to determine whether, in cells producing both types of pilus (doubly $\mathbf { R } ^ { + }$ cells), each pilus functions coordinately with the R factor specifying its formation. The experiment assumes that a pilus with one or more phage particles adsorbed to its tip will function less efficiently in mating than it would otherwise4. The doubly $\mathbb { R } ^ { + }$ donor was accordingly pretreated with a large excess of inactivated filamentous phage, either F-specific or I-specific. A phage that decreases the frequency of transfer of the other R factor would be acting non-specifically on the physiology of the cell. Experiments similar to this have been performed previously4 but, because the donor carried only one class of plasmid, the specific pilus-blocking efect could not be distinguished from the non-specific effect.
